876.title: Rattan Singh Bhangu
876.hook: his Panth Prakash told the Khalsa's hard century in verse
876.howItsDone: Rattan Singh Bhangu's Panth Prakash is read by Sikh historians and drawn on in gurdwara katha about the eighteenth century, alongside other sources.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three roads: Sikh chroniclers, Persian records, and memory. Your line was how do we know. Today, one of those chroniclers, by name.

A Sikh sits down to write. Not in prose. In verse, line after line that can be read aloud and remembered. He has the stories his family told him: the riders and the forests, the great killing, the temple blown up and rebuilt. Some of them are about his own family. And, by his own account, he has a reason to write: outsiders are asking about the Sikhs, and he wants the Sikh side told by a Sikh.
screen: `A SIKH WRITES IN VERSE.` → `STORIES HIS FAMILY TOLD HIM.` → `THE SIKH SIDE, TOLD BY A SIKH.`

segments.voice: First, the book. It's called Panth Prakash. Panth is the path, and the word Sikhs use for the whole community. Prakash is light, the shining of something into view. So the title promises to bring the Panth into the light. Second, why he wrote it. Bhangu says a British officer was collecting accounts of Sikh history, and that he heard the Sikhs described by people who didn't know them. So he set out to tell it from inside. That's a choice worth noticing. He didn't write an angry reply. He wrote the long story, with names, places and family memory, so it would be there for anyone who asked. Third, his family is in it. Bhangu traces his line to Mehtab Singh, one of the riders remembered for punishing the man who had turned the Harmandir into a place of drinking and dancing. So when he tells the hard century, he's telling his own family's world. Fourth, how to read him. Because he wrote later, from memory and family tradition, historians read him carefully, beside other sources: yesterday's lesson in action. And yet several stories on this path in recent weeks, Kapur Singh fanning the sangat, the boy Jassa Singh singing, the shaheedi bunga, are told in the forms Sikhs know through tellings like his. When this path says tradition says, Bhangu is one of the voices in that tradition. The chronicler.

segments.voice: Find or recall one line of history, a sentence from a book, a plaque on a building, an inscription on a gravestone, the first line of a page about where your family came from, and read it slowly, once. Then put it down, breathe, and ask who wrote it, and where they were standing. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out.

Your line: the chronicler. Every story you love was kept by someone. Day eight hundred seventy-six, and counting.

877.title: Remembering without hatred
877.hook: the Ardas names martyrs, not enemies; memory is for courage, not revenge
877.howItsDone: Sikhs stand for the Ardas at the close of services and daily prayers; one passage remembers the martyrs by what they endured, the congregation answers Waheguru, and the prayer closes asking for the good of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rattan Singh Bhangu, the chronicler who set the hard century down in verse so the Sikh side would be told. Today, what Sikhs do with all that memory.

Partway through the Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings, comes a passage that's hard to hear. It remembers Sikhs cut limb from limb, scalped, broken on the wheel, sawn apart, who gave their heads and kept their faith. The congregation stands with folded hands and answers Waheguru. And something is missing. The governors, the generals, the invaders who did these things: their names aren't there. Today: remembering without hatred.
screen: `THE ARDAS REMEMBERS THE MARTYRS.` → `CUT, SCALPED, BROKEN, SAWN.` → `AND NOT ONE ENEMY IS NAMED.`

segments.voice: Start with what the prayer keeps. The Ardas names the Gurus, the Sahibzade, the Panj Piare, and then the ones whose names are lost, by what they endured and what they held on to: their hair, their faith, their Guru. Memory pointed at the ones who stood, not the ones who struck. Second, a line Guru Arjan left in the Guru Granth Sahib, here in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. It comes from a Guru who was himself put to death, and it can be heard alongside the long list of martyrs. It doesn't say nothing bad happened. It says the heart doesn't have to be organized around the people who did it. Third, how the prayer ends. After all that suffering, the Ardas asks for sarbat da bhala, the good of all. Everyone, not everyone except them. A few weeks back, this path met a minister whose grief turned into a slaughter; Sikhs tell that story too. Read this way, the Ardas keeps grief from being handed on as hatred. When Sikhs stand and remember, the prayer doesn't ask who to pay back. It asks, in effect, could I stand like that? Courage, not revenge.
screen: `THE PRAYER NAMES THOSE WHO STOOD.` · `NO ONE IS MY ENEMY, NO ONE A STRANGER.` · `IT ENDS ASKING THE GOOD OF ALL.` · `HATRED IS NOT HANDED ON.` · then, large: `COURAGE, NOT REVENGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who went through something hard, in your family or your own life, and see it plainly. If your attention drifts to the one who caused it, bring it gently back to the one who endured: what did they hold on to? If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out; if not, let any anger pass like weather.
Ardas, the prayer said standing at the close of Sikh gatherings. It names the martyrs by what they endured, names no enemy, and ends asking the good of all. Today's word.

878.title: The Budha Dal today
878.hook: the Nihang army traces itself to the elders' Dal of this century
878.howItsDone: Nihang Sikhs live in Dals with their own leaders and moving camps, wear blue with high turbans, keep horses and practice gatka, and gather for Hola Mohalla at Anandpur.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ardas: it names the martyrs, not the enemies, and asks the good of all. Courage, not revenge. Today, riders who never left the saddle.

Deep blue robes. A turban wound high, almost a tower, ringed with steel circles and small blades. A spear in hand, a horse nearby, a voice calling out the Khalsa's victory cry. If you've seen photographs from the festival of Hola Mohalla at Anandpur, you may have seen them: the Nihangs. They can look like figures stepped out of an old painting. They aren't a reenactment. They say they are the same army that rode through the century you've been hearing about, still riding. Today: the Budha Dal today.
screen: `BLUE ROBES, A TOWERING TURBAN.` → `HOLA MOHALLA AT ANANDPUR.` → `THE SAME ARMY, STILL RIDING.`

segments.voice: A few weeks back on this path, the Khalsa organized its riders into two bodies: the Budha Dal, the army of the elders, and the Taruna Dal, the army of the young. Budha means old. The elders' Dal kept the camps, guarded the shrines, held the memory. The Nihang groups of today trace themselves to that body. One still carries the name Budha Dal, with its own jathedar, its own leader, and its own camps that move from place to place. In their telling, the line was never broken. Second, what they keep. Tradition says the Nihangs hold on to ways of the old riders that life elsewhere has left behind: the blue dress, the high turban with its weapons, moving camps, care for horses, the martial art called gatka, and a coded, joking way of speaking that belongs to the camps. Time with them shows the hard century as a practice, not a chapter. Third, honest complexity. There's more than one Nihang Dal today, and they don't all agree, with each other or with other Sikhs, about every practice. Sikhs hold a range of views about them. What's clear is the claim they make: the riders of the hard century didn't only leave descendants and stories. They left an army that still keeps its camp. The old army lives.

Picture them keeping it, and notice how easily it could have stopped with them. Rest there in gratitude, with Waheguru on each breath out if you pray.
Nihang. The order of Sikh warriors who say they are the elders' army of the hard century still riding: blue robes, high turbans, moving camps. Today's word.

879.title: Daily life on horseback
879.hook: cooking, praying and reading the Granth in camps
879.howItsDone: Sikhs say their daily prayers, the nitnem, morning, evening and night, often from memory or a small prayer book, wherever they are; at home, travel or work, the practice goes with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nihangs, who say the elders' army never broke camp. The old army lives. Today, what that camp's ordinary days were like.

Before dawn in a riders' camp. Horses stamping in the cold. Somebody blowing on last night's coals. Nobody knows yet whether today means a long ride, a fight, or a day hiding in tall grass. And before any of that is decided, voices start up, low, among the tents and blankets: the morning prayers, said from memory. The history books fill up with battles and sieges. Today is about the hours in between. Today: daily life on horseback.
screen: `BEFORE DAWN IN A RIDERS' CAMP.` → `NOBODY KNOWS WHAT THE DAY HOLDS.` → `THE MORNING PRAYERS, FROM MEMORY.`

segments.voice: Start with the prayers, because tradition puts them first. Guru Ram Das left a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib about a Sikh's day. In paraphrase: one who calls themselves a Sikh of the Guru rises early, bathes, and remembers the Name, and keeps remembering it sitting and standing through the day. Notice what it needs. No building, no fixed address. Water and a voice. The riders could carry it anywhere, and tradition says they knew the daily prayers by heart. Second, the Granth itself. Tradition says the bands carried copies of the scripture, wrapped and kept with care, and when the camp stopped, a place was made for it, and it was opened and read, the way it is in a gurdwara. A gurdwara, in a sense, could be pitched like a tent. Third, the food. Riders cooked what they could get: coarse bread, roasted grain, whatever a village shared. Tradition says even here it was cooked together and eaten together, sitting on the ground. Put the three side by side. The hunted years didn't stop Sikh practice. They made it portable: the prayers in memory, the scripture in a bundle, the shared meal around whatever fire there was. When the camp moved, all of it moved too. Prayer on the move.
screen: `RISE EARLY, REMEMBER THE NAME.` · `THE PRAYERS CARRIED BY HEART.` · `THE GRANTH OPENED WHEREVER THEY STOPPED.` · `COOKED TOGETHER, EATEN ON THE GROUND.` · then, large: `PRAYER ON THE MOVE.`

segments.voice: If you can, move to a different spot: the step outside, a chair by a window, or just turn to face another wall. Settle there and do what you usually do, a breath, a line of prayer, Waheguru if you pray, or simple silence. Notice how the place is different and the practice is the same.

880.title: Langar in hard times
880.hook: even hunted, the camps kept a shared kitchen
880.howItsDone: Gurdwaras keep langar, a free kitchen where volunteers cook and anyone may eat, sitting together on the floor; Sikhs give food, money and time to keep it running.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prayer on the move: prayers by heart, the Granth opened wherever the camp stopped. Today, the pot over the fire.

Rice cooked sweet with ghee, and a woman sharing it out to whoever sits down. That scene is in the Guru Granth Sahib, in a ballad by the musicians Satta and Balwand. The woman is Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife, and the place is the Guru's langar, the free kitchen. Generations later, the Khalsa was hunted through forests and marshes, with little flour to spare. So what happened to that kitchen? Today: langar in hard times.
screen: `SWEET RICE IN THE GURU'S KITCHEN.` → `MATA KHIVI IN THE SCRIPTURE.` → `THEN THE HUNTED YEARS.`

segments.voice: The ballad says, in paraphrase: Mata Khivi is a good woman whose shade is thick like a leafy tree, and in the Guru's langar, rich sweet rice is shared out. A woman feeding people made it into the scripture. The kitchen is holy ground. Then the hard century. Tradition says that even hunted, living in forests and moving at night, the bands kept a common pot. When there was little, the little was divided. And the old teaching held: anyone who came to the fire, Sikh or not, stranger or not, was fed. Ten days ago, on the coins struck at Lahore, you heard three words, deg, tegh, fateh: the pot, the sword, victory, with the pot first. In the camps that order was a daily habit, not a slogan. A band that couldn't protect its own village for a season could still share its bread. Tradition also says villagers who gave grain to the riders were fed from the same pot. In the stories, the kitchen was how the Khalsa stayed a people and not just an army. Langar was never only charity, the rich feeding the poor. In the hard century the cooks were poor too. They shared anyway: not waiting until there was plenty, but setting out what there was. Share it anyway.

segments.voice: Think about the food actually in your day: what's in the fridge, the snack in your bag, the lunch you're planning. Picture one person you could share a piece of it with, a coworker, a neighbor, someone at the door, and picture handing it over. If something in you clenches, let it loosen; if you pray, let Waheguru go out with each breath.

881.title: The Khalsa shall rule
881.hook: a couplet after Ardas speaks of the Khalsa ruling; Sikhs understand it in several ways, from justice to spiritual sovereignty
881.howItsDone: In gurdwaras the congregation often sings the couplet beginning raj karega Khalsa after the Ardas, standing, and Sikh teachers explain it as sovereignty, as just and gentle rule, and as mastery of the self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, langar in hard times: a common pot, deg before the sword. Share it anyway. Today, three words sung right after the Ardas.

The Ardas is over. The congregation is still standing, hands folded. Then the whole room sings a short couplet together, loud and steady. It opens with three words in Punjabi: raj karega Khalsa. The Khalsa shall rule. For a visitor hearing it the first time, it can land with a jolt. Rule over whom? Rule how? Fair questions, and Sikhs themselves answer them in more than one way.
screen: `AFTER THE ARDAS, A SUNG COUPLET.` → `RAJ KAREGA KHALSA.` → `RULE OVER WHOM? RULE HOW?`

segments.voice: Where it comes from: the couplet isn't in the Guru Granth Sahib. Tradition attributes it to Guru Gobind Singh, and it's recorded in one of the old codes of Sikh conduct. Its next lines say, in paraphrase, that none will stay defiant, that those who wandered in misery will come together, and that those who take shelter will be safe. Tradition says it was sung through the hunted century by people with a price on their heads. That's the first way Sikhs hear it: a promise of sovereignty, said aloud when it looked impossible, and remembered later when Sikh chiefs did hold the land. The second way is justice. Guru Arjan, in the Guru Granth Sahib, describes a rule where, in paraphrase, by the merciful one's command no one pushes another around, no one hurts another, and everyone lives at ease. He calls it halemi raj, a gentle rule. Some readers hear the couplet through that line: a rule where nobody is crushed. The third way turns inward. Khalsa can mean the pure, those who belong directly to the Guru. In this reading, the first kingdom to rule is the self: anger, greed, ego, fear. Someone who can't rule their own temper isn't ready to rule anything else. These readings don't cancel each other. Sikhs hold them side by side, and different gurdwaras and teachers lean different ways. The third is the one anyone can try today. Rule yourself first.
screen: `A PROMISE SUNG WHILE HUNTED.` · `HALEMI RAJ: A GENTLE RULE.` · `THE FIRST KINGDOM IS THE SELF.` · `READINGS HELD SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `RULE YOURSELF FIRST.`

segments.voice: Ask one plain question: what in me tends to take over, temper in traffic, the phone at midnight, worry that runs the morning? Name just one, then picture the next time it rises and, for one breath, choosing what happens next, not crushing it, just being the one in charge. If you pray, rest in Waheguru as you breathe.

882.title: Visiting the sites
882.hook: gurdwaras now mark Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira
882.howItsDone: Gurdwaras stand at Kahnuwan and Kup Rahira; Sikhs visit to pray and remember the two ghallugharas, and the anniversaries are marked there with readings, kirtan and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, raj karega Khalsa: sovereignty, halemi raj the gentle rule, and ruling the self. Today, two places in the fields.

Flat fields. Wheat, or mustard in its season, running to the edge of sight. An irrigation channel, a dirt road, a tractor parked by a wall. And in the middle of it, a white building with a dome and a tall flagpole, the saffron Nishan Sahib lifting in the wind. If you didn't know the story, you'd see a village gurdwara like any other. But this ground has a name in Sikh memory. Today: visiting the sites.
screen: `FLAT FIELDS, A DIRT ROAD.` → `A WHITE DOME, A SAFFRON FLAG.` → `GROUND WITH A NAME IN MEMORY.`

segments.voice: The first place is Kahnuwan, near the marshes where, a few weeks back, families and riders were trapped in the smaller holocaust, the chhota ghallughara. Ghallughara means a great destruction. Chhota means small, though nothing about it was small to those who lived it. Today a gurdwara stands there, and Sikhs come to remember. The second is Kup Rahira, where the Khalsa made a moving ring around its families and the great holocaust, the vadda ghallughara, fell on them. A gurdwara marks that ground too. Now notice what stands at the heart of each site. Not a battle trophy. Not a wall of grievance. A gurdwara: the Guru Granth Sahib opened, hymns sung, and a langar feeding anyone who walks in. The memorial is a working kitchen. That fits this whole week: memory pointed at courage, the pot before the sword. And the sites hold a quiet lesson. The fields came back. Crops grow right up to the gurdwara walls. A child can grow up within sight of it and learn the story from the person who serves them tea there. The places hold what happened, so the people who live there don't carry it alone. This week: Rattan Singh Bhangu, remembering without hatred, the Budha Dal today, daily life on horseback, langar in hard times, the Khalsa shall rule, and visiting the sites. The places remember.
screen: `KAHNUWAN: THE SMALLER HOLOCAUST.` · `KUP RAHIRA: THE GREAT HOLOCAUST.` · `NOT A MONUMENT, A GURDWARA.` · `THE FIELDS CAME BACK.` · then, large: `THE PLACES REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: If you have a phone nearby, open a map and find Kahnuwan or Kup Rahira; zoom in until you see the fields and roads, then put it down and close your eyes. Hold that ordinary ground and what tradition says happened there, or simply picture the white dome in the fields. If you pray, say Waheguru softly on each breath out.
